abstract.p: This epitaph commemorates the death of the speaker’s “sister,” the Lady Vayne, and addresses a passing stranger. The poem argues that souls (not bodies) define true kinship, and that goodness is what makes souls related. Because she was virtuous, her soul has already received its reward in heaven, while the living are still striving toward it. She now joins the heavenly choir, enjoying what others can only hope for. The speaker ends by urging the reader that, if they are also good, they should pray that their soul may join hers. The Latin line means something like “May it be granted to me to live and die in this way.”

Sir Richarads Anderson his Epitaph on the death
of his Sister the Lady Vayne
app.rdg: Sir R. Anderson's Epitaph upon his sister the L. Vayne

lg.l: Stay strainger know if good thou bee, he
Heers one buried one neere kinne to thee;
Soules worthier then our bodies bin,
And goodness ‘tis mak’s soules of kinne:
Good soules have all one end and scope,
And hers injoyes what ours but hope.
Goodnes hath there its meerite found;
So whylst wee fight, her soule is crowned:
And singes forth Hymns in that blest quire
To which all good soules doe aspire.
Goe strainger now if good thou art,
Pray thine with hers may beare a parte.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Elizabeth Spencer (christened 30 November 1589), commemorated in this epitaph as “Lady Vayne” (or Fane), was the daughter of Robert Spencer, 1st Baron Spencer of Wormleighton. She was the sister of Mary Spencer, who married Sir Richard Anderson, making Elizabeth his sister-in-law, though the poem refers to her simply as his “sister.” She married George Fane on 3 September 1607, and the marriage produced no children. She died in 1618, aged 28, and was buried on 19 November in St Nicholas’s Chapel, Westminster Abbey, where a large alabaster and marble monument commemorates her ().
